## Overview

The BigThaw reanalysis data used in our analysis may be subject to error. While precipitation measures have been cross-validated and corrected for, temperature data requires further investigation. Here, I compare daily BigThaw reanalysis data with daily observational from the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) for 4 sites within Himachal Pradesh India (i.e. Bhuntar, Larji, Manali and Pandoh) between the years 1998 to 2004 and 2014 to 2017.

Please note that observational data is difficult to access in India and not available for the sites examined in our main analysis. This preliminary analysis does not contain a complete time series since I wanted to gauge error using time frames readily available on the JASMIN portal. The final iteration of this should include a complete time series from 1998 to 2017. The IMD data only contains daily maximum and minimum temperature, and not averages.

## Basic deviations

Upon first glance, the BigThaw dataset measures temperature 4.6 (minimum temperature) and 3.4 (maximum temperature) degrees lower than the in-situ data. This mean error deviates across the provided locations, with Bhuntar having the least amount of error and Manali having the greatest.

```{r, echo=FALSE}

# 1. Basic deviation (bias, error magnitude, agreement) #####

compute_metrics <- function(obs, model) {
  err <- model - obs
  n   <- sum(!is.na(err))
  tibble(
    n     = n,
    ME    = mean(err, na.rm = TRUE),                       # mean bias (systematic error)
    MAE   = mean(abs(err), na.rm = TRUE),                  # mean absolute error
    RMSE  = sqrt(mean(err^2, na.rm = TRUE)),                # root mean sq error
    r     = cor(obs, model, use = "complete.obs"),          # linear association
    sd_IMD   = sd(obs, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_BigThaw = sd(model, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}

metrics_mn2t <- compute_metrics(df$mn2t_imd, df$mn2t_bt)
metrics_mx2t <- compute_metrics(df$mx2t_imd, df$mx2t_bt)

metrics_by_station <- df %>%
  group_by(location) %>%
  summarise(
    n     = sum(!is.na(mn2t_bt - mn2t_imd)),
    ME_mn    = mean(mn2t_bt - mn2t_imd, na.rm = TRUE),
    RMSE_mn  = sqrt(mean((mn2t_bt - mn2t_imd)^2, na.rm = TRUE)),
    ME_mx    = mean(mx2t_bt - mx2t_imd, na.rm = TRUE),
    RMSE_mx  = sqrt(mean((mx2t_bt - mx2t_imd)^2, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(RMSE_mx))

# Pooled tables: tag with variable + a "Pooled" location so they stack cleanly
pooled <- bind_rows(
  metrics_mn2t %>% mutate(variable = "mn2t", location = "Pooled"),
  metrics_mx2t %>% mutate(variable = "mx2t", location = "Pooled")
)

# Per-station table: pivot to long format so ME/RMSE align with pooled columns
station_long <- metrics_by_station %>%
  select(location, n, ME_mn, RMSE_mn, ME_mx, RMSE_mx) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(location, n),
    names_to = c(".value", "variable"),
    names_sep = "_"
  ) %>%
  mutate(variable = paste0(variable, "2t"))

# Combine
combined <- bind_rows(pooled, station_long) %>%
  select(variable, location, n, ME, MAE, RMSE, r, sd_IMD, sd_BigThaw) %>%
  arrange(variable, location != "Pooled", location)

fmt_na <- function(x) {
  ifelse(is.na(x), " ", sprintf("%.2f", x))
}

combined %>%
  select(-variable) %>%
  mutate(across(c(ME, MAE, RMSE, r, sd_IMD, sd_BigThaw), fmt_na)) %>%
  kbl(
    col.names = c("Location", "n", "ME", "MAE", "RMSE", "r", "SD (IMD)", "SD (BigThaw)"),
    caption = "Reanalysis Deviation Metrics: Pooled and Per-Station",
    align = "lrrrrrrr"
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
  pack_rows("mn2t", 1, sum(combined$variable == "mn2t")) %>%
  pack_rows("mx2t", sum(combined$variable == "mn2t") + 1, nrow(combined)) %>%
  row_spec(which(combined$location == "Pooled"), bold = TRUE)
```

## Temporal deviations

These deviations likely vary over time, particularly month and year. We find that mean error is lowest in May and June and highest in February and October. The difference between datasets is broadly comparable over the years, with few exceptions. Notably, 2004 has a much greater difference (\>6 degrees) and 2014 has a much smaller difference (\<2 degrees). It also important to note all variables across datasets have autocorrelation that needs to be accounted for when we quantify errors.

```{r, echo=FALSE}

# Bias by month
seasonal_bias <- df %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    ME_mx2t = mean(mx2t_bt - mx2t_imd, na.rm = TRUE),
    ME_mn2t = mean(mn2t_bt - mn2t_imd, na.rm = TRUE),
    RMSE_mx2t = sqrt(mean((mx2t_bt - mx2t_imd)^2, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(seasonal_bias, aes(x = factor(month, levels = month.abb), y = ME_mx2t)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkblue") +
  labs(title = "Monthly mean bias in mx2t (BT - IMD)", x = "Month", y = "Bias (°C)") +
  theme_minimal()

# Bias by year
yearly_bias <- df %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(ME_mx2t = mean(mx2t_bt - mx2t_imd, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(yearly_bias, aes(x = year, y = ME_mx2t)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkred") +
  labs(title = "Yearly mean bias in mx2t (BT - IMD)", x = "Year", y = "Bias (°C)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Statistical bias metrics

We first used a block bootstrap to statistically quantify the uncertainty between data sets because it allowed us to preserve autocorrelation structures (i.e. lags up to 10). We found the bootstrapped bias to be very similar to those identified in the basic errors calculated above, with significant CI values.

Bland-Altman agreement plots help visualise the agreement between two measurements. These plots include a the mean difference (blue) between paired measurements on the x- and y-axes and the 95% limits of the agreement (red). This further confirms the high degree of disagreement between BigThaw and IMD measurements for both temperature measures, but suggests the CI limits of agreement are wider than the boot straped values.

Finally to test if the differences between methods were systematic, I also fit a Deming regression. This method accounts for measurement uncertainty in both the independent and dependent variables, thus making it appropriate for method comparison. Here we test the null hypothesis that the two methods are equivalent within the measured range (i.e. no systematic differences detected). We find that both the intercept and slope indicate fail to reject this hypothesis since the CI' do not cross 0 for the intercept, nor do they cross 1 for the slope.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# 3. Block bootstrap with CI for bias metrics ####

## Moving block bootstrap: resample contiguous blocks of days
## (preserves short-term autocorrelation structure) rather than
## resampling individual days independently.

block_bootstrap_ci <- function(obs, model, block_len = 10, R = 2000) {
  err <- model - obs
  err <- err[!is.na(err)]
  n <- length(err)
  n_blocks <- ceiling(n / block_len)
  
  stat_fun <- function(data, indices) {
    # indices select block START points; build resampled series from blocks
    resampled <- unlist(lapply(indices, function(i) {
      end <- min(i + block_len - 1, n)
      data[i:end]
    }))
    c(ME = mean(resampled), RMSE = sqrt(mean(resampled^2)))
  }
  
  starts <- 1:(n - block_len + 1)
  boot_out <- boot(
    data = err,
    statistic = function(data, i) stat_fun(data, sample(starts, n_blocks, replace = TRUE)),
    R = R
  )
  
  ci_ME   <- boot.ci(boot_out, type = "perc", index = 1)$percent[4:5]
  ci_RMSE <- boot.ci(boot_out, type = "perc", index = 2)$percent[4:5]
  
  list(
    ME_est   = mean(err), ME_CI   = ci_ME,
    RMSE_est = sqrt(mean(err^2)), RMSE_CI = ci_RMSE,
    boot_out = boot_out
  )
}

ci_mx2t <- block_bootstrap_ci(df$mx2t_imd, df$mx2t_bt, block_len = 10, R = 2000)
ci_mn2t <- block_bootstrap_ci(df$mn2t_imd, df$mn2t_bt, block_len = 10, R = 2000)

cat("BOOTSTRAPPED MN2T \nmn2t bias:", round(ci_mn2t$ME_est,3),
    " 95% CI:", round(ci_mn2t$ME_CI,3), "\n")
cat("mn2t RMSE:", round(ci_mn2t$RMSE_est,3),
    " 95% CI:", round(ci_mn2t$RMSE_CI,3), "\n")

cat("BOOTSTRAPPED MX2T \nmx2t bias:", round(ci_mx2t$ME_est,3),
    " 95% CI:", round(ci_mx2t$ME_CI,3), "\n")
cat("mx2t RMSE:", round(ci_mx2t$RMSE_est,3),
    " 95% CI:", round(ci_mx2t$RMSE_CI,3), "\n")


## block_len choice: pick roughly the decorrelation length seen in the
## ACF plot above (e.g. if ACF drops off after ~5-10 lags, block_len=10 is reasonable)


```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# 2. Bland-Altman agreement analysis ####

## Shows whether disagreement depends on the magnitude of temperature
## (e.g. reanalysis might be fine in mid-range temps but diverge at extremes)

bland_altman_plot <- function(obs, model, varname) {
  d <- tibble(
    mean_val = (obs + model) / 2,
    diff_val = model - obs
  ) %>% drop_na()
  
  bias <- mean(d$diff_val)
  sdiff <- sd(d$diff_val)
  loa_upper <- bias + 1.96 * sdiff
  loa_lower <- bias - 1.96 * sdiff
  
  ggplot(d, aes(mean_val, diff_val)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = bias, color = "darkblue") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = loa_upper, color = "darkred", linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = loa_lower, color = "darkred", linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(title = paste("Bland-Altman:", varname),
         subtitle = paste0("Bias=", round(bias,2),
                           "  Limits of agreement=[", round(loa_lower,2),
                           ", ", round(loa_upper,2), "]"),
         x = "Mean of IMD & BT (°C)", y = "BT - IMD (°C)") +
    theme_minimal()
}

print(bland_altman_plot(df$mn2t_imd, df$mn2t_bt, "Min. Temperature"))
print(bland_altman_plot(df$mx2t_imd, df$mx2t_bt, "Max. Temperature"))


```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# 5. Deming regression analysis (errors-in-variables) ####

## Ordinary least squares assumes the x-axis variable is error-free.
## Since BOTH IMD and BT carry uncertainty, Deming regression is more
## appropriate than OLS for assessing systematic (proportional) bias.

deming_mx2t <- deming(mx2t_bt ~ mx2t_imd, data = df)
print(deming_mx2t)
# Slope != 1 or intercept != 0 indicates systematic (not just random) bias


```

## Conclusion

This initial analysis suggests that we have systematic error in the BigThaw data that we need to address. The tests I provide here are my first stab at comparing the deviations in data, and I would appreciate any additional tests to improve this assessment. I am also not familiar with the best approach to calibrating data once the systematic error is quantified, so guidance on that would also be appreciated.
